stories.label: UK shelves Chagos Islands deal after Trump's criticism
stories.summary: Britain promised to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius — ending 60 years of displacement of the Chagossian people — then shelved the deal after Trump called it 'great stupidity.' The real story: Diego Garcia hosts a US-UK military base critical to Indian Ocean power projection, and Washington vetoed decolonization to keep it. Lead with the Chagossians who were expelled and still cannot return. The sentiment divergence (0.71) shows sources disagree sharply on framing — Middle East Eye calls it colonial, Express calls it a U-turn victory.

stories.label: US agrees to unfreeze Iranian funds abroad - media
stories.summary: The US reportedly agreed to release $6 billion in Iranian assets frozen in Qatar and other banks — the most concrete concession signal since Islamabad talks began. Iran called it a sign of 'seriousness.' Lead with the dollar figure and what it buys: this is the same $6B that was controversially unfrozen then refrozen after October 2023. The mechanism matters — who holds the funds, what conditions attach, and whether this survives Congressional backlash.

stories.label: Pakistani fighter jets land in Saudi Arabia as part of defence pact
stories.summary: Pakistan deployed fighter jets to Saudi Arabia under a mutual defense pact on the same day it hosts US-Iran peace talks in Islamabad. The juxtaposition is the story: Islamabad is simultaneously mediating peace and arming one side's neighbor. Lead with the timing — jets landing at King Abdulaziz Air Base while diplomats sit across the table 2,000km away. This reveals Pakistan's hedging strategy and the Saudi-Pakistan defense axis strengthening during the Iran war.

stories.label: Easter truce between Russia, Ukraine begins
stories.summary: Russia and Ukraine began an Easter ceasefire and exchanged 350 POWs (175 each, plus 7 Kursk civilians) — the largest prisoner swap in months. Kyiv warned it would respond 'immediately' to violations. Lead with the POW numbers and the fragility: Putin ordered the truce, Zelenskyy agreed reluctantly, and neither side expects it to hold. The reader should understand this as a humanitarian window, not a peace signal.

stories.label: Pilots' union calls strikes at Lufthansa on April 13, 14
stories.summary: Lufthansa pilots will strike Monday-Tuesday across Lufthansa Cargo, CityLine, and Eurowings after management showed 'no discernible willingness to reach a solution.' This hits European air travel during an already constrained jet fuel market from the Iran war. Lead with the compounding effect: fuel prices up 40%+ from Hormuz disruption, and now the largest European carrier's pilots walk out. The labor angle — pilots pushing back against post-pandemic contract erosion — matters for economy readers.

stories.label: Crypto TradFi perpetuals are predicting the direction of Wall Street's Monday open with 89% accuracy
stories.summary: Crypto perpetual futures now predict Monday's Wall Street direction with 89% accuracy, and weekend trading volume has grown to 38% of weekday levels. This is a structural shift: price discovery no longer stops when NYSE closes. Lead with the 89% figure and what it means — crypto markets are becoming the de facto weekend pricing layer for traditional finance. Binance leads volume. The Iran war's weekend volatility accelerated adoption.

stories.label: BREAKING: Nigerian govt releases updated list of terrorism financiers
stories.summary: Nigeria's sanctions committee published a list of 48 individuals and armed groups financing terrorism — including Islamic State West Africa Province and Boko Haram networks. The accountability mechanism matters: naming financiers publicly is how you choke funding. Lead with the 48 names and what groups they fund. The reader should see this as Nigeria taking ownership of its counterterrorism architecture rather than outsourcing it to the US or UN.

stories.label: Irish bog plant revives ancient remedy as a new weapon vs superbugs
stories.summary: Researchers found that compounds from an Irish bog plant used in traditional medicine are effective against antibiotic-resistant superbugs. Lead with the antimicrobial resistance crisis — 1.27 million deaths annually from drug-resistant infections — and the irony that a pre-modern remedy may help solve a modern crisis. The science reader wants the mechanism: which compounds, which pathogens, how does resistance differ from synthetic antibiotics.

stories.label: EFF is leaving X
stories.summary: The Electronic Frontier Foundation — the internet's most prominent digital rights organization — announced it is leaving X (Twitter). 1,415 HN points, 1,282 comments. Lead with what EFF is and why this matters: the organization that has defended online speech for 35 years concluded that the platform no longer serves that mission. This is not a political boycott — it's a structural judgment about X's role in the digital rights ecosystem. The Grok nudification scandal (covered last cycle) is part of the context.

stories.label: Iran unable to find mines in Strait of Hormuz, US says
stories.summary: Iran mined the Strait of Hormuz during the war but now can't locate all the mines it placed — the strait is nominally open but functionally closed because the country that mined it lost control of its own minefield. Lead with the absurdity: Iran offered 'safe routes' but US officials say the IRGC's own maps are unreliable. 6 tankers passed Thursday, zero on Wednesday, despite the ceasefire. The reader tracking the war's economic fallout will see why 'ceasefire' doesn't mean 'recovery' — this is the mine problem that no peace deal can solve quickly.

stories.label: 'Abhorrent': the inside story of the Polymarket gamblers betting millions on war
stories.summary: Guardian investigation reveals how anonymous Polymarket gamblers bet millions on war outcomes — and how their disputes over 'truth' (which frontline map is authoritative, whether a ceasefire counts) are reshaping how news gets arbitrated. Lead with the mechanism: prediction markets don't just bet on events, they create financial incentives to define what happened. The reader who follows both crypto markets and the Iran/Ukraine wars will see the collision of gambling, information warfare, and journalism.

stories.label: Record number of homes in Great Britain turn to green energy as fuel prices soar
stories.summary: British households are installing solar panels, heat pumps, and buying EVs at record rates — driven not by climate conviction but by the Iran war sending energy bills up 18% from July. Lead with the inversion: war, not policy, is accomplishing what years of green subsidies couldn't. The reader tracking the Iran war's economic cascade will see the demand-side response: when fossil fuel prices spike hard enough, consumers switch — and the energy transition gets an accidental accelerant.

stories.label: India news: Delhi plans fossil fuel bike ban by 2028
stories.summary: Delhi — one of the world's most polluted cities — plans to ban new petrol two-wheelers from 2028, with road tax waivers and scrapping incentives up to ₹1 lakh for EVs. Lead with the scale: two-wheelers are 70%+ of Delhi's registered vehicles and the single largest source of transport emissions. The reader will see a Global South megacity making the most aggressive EV mandate yet — not for climate branding, but because the air is literally unbreathable.

stories.label: Plastic Pollution Is Bad Enough. Burning It Can Be Even Worse.
stories.summary: In Indonesia, plastic waste is burned in unregulated low-tech furnaces — and the health consequences are far worse than landfilling. Even incinerators with air scrubbers are linked to premature birth and congenital abnormalities, but open burning in the Global South produces orders of magnitude more dioxins and furans. Lead with the health data: birth defects near burning sites. The reader will see the hidden cost of the global plastic waste trade — wealthy nations export plastic, poorer nations burn it, and the health burden falls on communities with no regulatory protection.

stories.label: 'Poor man's Majoranas' can be used as quantum spin probes
stories.summary: Researchers found that 'poor man's Majorana' quasiparticles — easier to create than the elusive real Majorana fermions — can serve as quantum spin probes, opening a practical path to quantum sensing without waiting for the particle physics breakthrough. Lead with the workaround: instead of hunting for a particle that may not exist in nature, physicists built a usable approximation from solid-state materials. The reader in tech will see the engineering pragmatism — shipping with what works rather than waiting for perfection.

stories.label: Senator launches inquiry into 8 tech giants for failures to adequately report CSAM
stories.summary: A US senator is investigating 8 major tech companies for deficient reporting of child sexual abuse material, following NCMEC reports alleging the platforms are also failing to report data on generative AI's role in producing CSAM. Lead with the AI connection: this isn't just about under-reporting known images — it's about platforms failing to track how their own generative AI tools are being used to create new abuse material. The reader will see the gap between the UK's criminal liability approach (covered previously with Ofcom/nudification) and the US congressional inquiry approach.

stories.label: US Intelligence Shows China Set to Supply Iran Arms, CNN Reports
stories.summary: US intelligence shows China preparing to ship MANPADS — shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles — to Iran within weeks. This is the first direct Chinese arms transfer to Iran during the war, transforming a bilateral US-Iran conflict into a potential proxy confrontation between the world's two largest economies. Lead with the MANPADS: cheap missiles that could threaten low-flying US aircraft and raise the cost of American air operations without triggering a direct China-US confrontation. The reader tracking the Iran war will see Beijing making a calculated bet — and the structural question of what happens when a third great power picks a side.

stories.label: Mamdani, Leaning Into 'Sewer Socialism,' Gets His Hands Dirty
stories.summary: At 100 days, NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani — the city's first Muslim mayor — is governing through 'sewer socialism': fixing public services instead of chasing big-ticket projects. Lead with the concept: a century-old socialist municipal tradition being revived by a Muslim-American mayor in the country's largest city. The reader will see practical, constituent-focused governance that contrasts sharply with the federal dysfunction they follow daily. The structural question: can a mayor who fixes sewers and bus routes build a political model that outlasts the culture wars?

stories.label: Bhutan has sold 70% of its bitcoin in 18 months. It may have stopped BTC mining too.
stories.summary: Bhutan has quietly sold 70% of its sovereign bitcoin holdings — $22.68M transferred Thursday alone — and may have stopped mining entirely. This was the most unusual government crypto experiment in the world: hydropower-mined bitcoin as a sovereign wealth strategy for a nation of 780,000 people. Lead with the unwinding: the real-world test of sovereign bitcoin adoption is ending in retreat. The reader who follows crypto and macro will see what happens when a small state bets on a volatile asset and the numbers stop working.

stories.label: Egypt's Lucky raises $23m to expand credit services and regional growth
stories.summary: Egyptian fintech Lucky raised $23M to expand credit services — one of the largest MENA fintech rounds in 2026. Lead with the market signal: while GCC economies reel from the Iran war and Gulf tourism collapses, Egypt's startup ecosystem is attracting growth capital for consumer credit. The reader tracking MENA tech will see a bet on Egypt's 100M+ population and massive unbanked majority — fintech as the financial infrastructure the state never built.

stories.label: DeBriefed 10 April 2026: Worst energy crisis 'ever' | India withdraws COP33 bid | Drag artists and climate change
stories.summary: India has withdrawn its bid to host COP33 — the world's third-largest carbon emitter stepping back from climate leadership as the Iran war triggers what the IEA calls the worst energy crisis ever. Lead with the withdrawal: India's retreat signals that climate diplomacy is losing ground to the immediate politics of energy costs and war-driven fuel disruption. The reader will see the connection: the same conflict driving $4/gallon gas is now dismantling the institutional architecture for addressing the climate crisis.

stories.label: Why Do We Tell Ourselves Scary Stories About AI?
stories.summary: Cognitive scientists are unpacking why humans project survival instincts, resource-hoarding, and manipulation onto AI systems — finding that our doom scenarios say more about human psychology than about what language models actually do. Lead with the inversion: the narratives that dominate AI discourse (scheming, deception, self-preservation) map onto evolved human threat-detection circuits, not onto anything the models exhibit. The reader who works in tech and navigates AI hype daily will see their own industry's narratives dissected through cognitive science.

stories.label: UK government threatens tech bosses with jail time if they do not adequately fight nudification tools
stories.summary: UK regulator Ofcom will threaten tech executives with prison if they fail to combat AI nudification tools — a direct response to the Grok scandal that produced millions of deepfake nude images of women and children. Lead with the criminal liability: the UK is making individual executives personally responsible for AI-generated sexual abuse imagery on their platforms. The reader will see the sharpest regulatory response yet to generative AI harms — and the question of whether personal criminal risk changes tech company behavior where fines haven't.

stories.label: Pakistani MFA expects constructive talks between US, Iran
stories.summary: Vance and Ghalibaf sit down in Islamabad on day 31+ of the US-Iran war — the first direct senior-level talks since hostilities began. Iran insists on a Lebanon ceasefire as precondition; the US wants nuclear concessions Tehran has already ruled out. Lead with the structural mismatch: both sides came to the table, but their opening positions are incompatible. The reader tracking the Iran war will see Pakistan's emergence as mediator — hosting talks that neither Geneva nor Doha could — while the ceasefire remains fragile and the Strait of Hormuz is still effectively closed.

stories.label: Conscientious objections to war rise sharply in US
stories.summary: March alone saw 80+ new conscientious objector cases — nearly double the annual norm. Service members cite the Minab school bombing as the turning point. Lead with the 80-in-one-month number against the usual annual pace — this is the sharpest spike in CO applications since Vietnam. The reader who opposes the war will see dissent emerging from inside the military itself, not just from protesters. The structural question: what happens to a volunteer military when its own soldiers refuse to fight?

stories.label: Los Angeles schools may close as nearly 85% of district's workers plan to strike
stories.summary: Nearly 85% of LAUSD workers — teachers, custodians, bus drivers — plan to strike next week while the district reportedly sits on $5 billion in reserves. Lead with the $5bn reserve number against the workers' pay demands: this isn't a broke district, it's a political choice. 600,000+ students in the second-largest US school district could lose school. The reader will see this as the austerity-vs-labor pattern playing out at massive scale.

stories.label: Could US-Iran talks in Islamabad bring gas prices back down?
stories.summary: Only 6 tankers passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday — zero on Wednesday — even after the ceasefire. Iranian attacks cut the Saudi East-West Pipeline by 10%, destroying the market's main workaround. Americans still pay $4+/gallon despite Brent crude dropping 10%. Lead with the 6-tanker number: the strait is nominally open but functionally closed, and mines plus US sanctions ambiguity are keeping ships away. The reader will see that even a peace deal won't bring quick relief — this is a logistics shock layered on a production shock.

stories.label: Federal judge blocks Arizona from bringing criminal charges against Kalshi
stories.summary: A federal judge blocked Arizona from criminally prosecuting prediction market Kalshi — the first time a state's gambling laws have been preempted by federal derivatives regulation. Lead with the collision: Arizona says it's gambling, the CFTC says it's a regulated market, and the court sided with the feds. The reader who follows prediction markets (and war bets, per previous coverage) will see the regulatory framework crystallizing: states can't shut down federally approved event contracts.

stories.label: Four astronauts are back home after a daring ride around the Moon
stories.summary: Artemis II splashed down safely off California — the first crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit in 54 years, breaking Apollo 13's distance record by 4,000+ miles. Lead with the splashdown: Orion hit the atmosphere at 25,000 mph and survived. The reader who follows space will care about the engineering milestone; the reader watching a divided America will note this was the one thing the country watched together during a war.

stories.label: AI and drones can select the most resilient wheat
stories.summary: Researchers combined drone imaging with AI to identify the wheat varieties most resilient to climate stress — faster and more accurate than traditional field trials. Lead with the practical application: as climate change threatens global wheat yields, this method lets breeders select drought-resistant varieties in a fraction of the time. The reader who works in tech will appreciate the AI application; the reader tracking food security will see the tool that could matter most for the next decade of harvests.

stories.label: Californians sue over AI tool that records doctor visits
stories.summary: A class-action lawsuit alleges Sutter Health and MemorialCare deployed Abridge's AI transcription tool to record patient visits without consent — violating California and federal wiretap laws. Lead with the mechanism: patients walked into a doctor's office and an AI was silently transcribing everything they said. The reader who builds software will recognize the consent failure pattern; the healthcare privacy implications are immediate and systemic as AI scribes proliferate across US hospitals.

stories.label: Israel strike kills 13 members of Lebanon state security
stories.summary: Israel killed 13 Lebanese state security personnel in a single airstrike on the Nabatieh Government Complex — the largest number of government employees killed at once since the war began. The angle: this isn't Hezbollah, these are civil servants at a government building. Lead with the distinction between militia and state targets — Israel is now striking the Lebanese government itself. The reader tracking the ceasefire will see that the two-week US-Iran truce has not stopped Israeli operations in Lebanon, which is exactly why Tehran set a Lebanon ceasefire as a precondition for talks.

stories.label: "Not Guns for Hire": Trump's Failure to Trigger a Kurdish Uprising
stories.summary: The US tried to enlist newly allied Kurdish factions to open a second front against Iran from inside Iraq — and the Kurds refused. The angle: this fills a glaring Iraq coverage gap. Lead with the refusal itself — a US proxy strategy that failed because the proxies had their own calculus. The reader tracking the Iran war will see that US leverage has limits even with allies it just armed, and that Iraq is not a passive theater.

stories.label: Sudan Nashra: Nyala healthcare workers on strike | Burhan abolishes deputy, assistant commander-in-chief positions | Sudanese military intelligence head in high-level talks with Tripoli's chief of staff | Military operation to retake Blue Nile's Kurmuk underway
stories.summary: Healthcare workers in Nyala, South Darfur are striking while Burhan consolidates military command by abolishing deputy positions and promoting hardliner Yasser al-Atta to chief of staff. Simultaneously, a military operation to retake Kurmuk on the Blue Nile is underway. The angle: Sudan's civil war is intensifying on multiple fronts — a healthcare collapse in the west, a military offensive in the east, and a command reshuffle that signals Burhan is choosing escalation over negotiation. Lead with the Nyala healthcare strike — civilians are losing medical access in a war zone while the generals restructure for more fighting.

stories.label: DOJ wants to scrap Watergate-era rule that makes presidential records public
stories.summary: The Trump DOJ is moving to dismantle the Presidential Records Act — the post-Watergate law that ensures presidential documents become public. The angle: this is accountability infrastructure being dismantled. Lead with what disappears if this succeeds — future historians, journalists, and FOIA requesters lose access to the documentary record of presidential decision-making. The reader who cares about transparency will see this as a structural erosion, not just a Trump story.

stories.label: Federal court hears new case against Trump's latest global tariffs
stories.summary: A three-judge panel at the US Court of International Trade heard oral arguments challenging Trump's sweeping global tariffs, with plaintiffs arguing he exceeded emergency powers meant for narrow crises. The angle: this is a constitutional test of whether a president can unilaterally restructure global trade under emergency authority. Lead with the legal mechanism — IEEPA was designed for sanctions on hostile states, not blanket import taxes on allies. The reader tracking trade policy will see this as the strongest legal challenge yet to the tariff regime.

stories.label: Govt reduces petrol price by Rs12 per litre, diesel by Rs135
stories.summary: Pakistan's PM Shehbaz Sharif announced a Rs135/litre diesel price cut in a televised address he called 'historic.' The angle: this is a massive government intervention — diesel down ~40% — timed to the Iran-US ceasefire and aimed at absorbing the economic shock that has battered Pakistani consumers for a month. Lead with the Rs135 number — it's the largest single fuel price cut in Pakistan's history. The reader tracking the Iran war's economic cascade (PIA, medicine, fuel) will see this as Pakistan desperately trying to stabilize before the Islamabad peace talks begin.

stories.label: White House warns staff over Iran war bets
stories.summary: The White House issued a warning to staff against using insider information on the Iran war to trade on prediction markets and financial markets, after repeated market spikes before major presidential announcements. The angle: the war isn't just geopolitics — it's a trading opportunity for those with advance knowledge of ceasefire announcements and escalation decisions. Lead with the pattern: markets spiked before several Trump announcements, suggesting someone was front-running war decisions. The reader who follows markets will immediately grasp the corruption mechanism.

stories.label: Marine heatwaves 'nearly double' the economic damage caused by tropical cyclones
stories.summary: Tropical cyclones that pass over marine heatwaves become 'supercharged,' nearly doubling their economic damage. The angle: climate change isn't just making storms worse in a vague sense — marine heatwaves are a specific, measurable amplifier with a dollar figure attached. Lead with the doubling — this quantifies the climate-disaster feedback loop in a way that connects ocean temperatures directly to insurance losses and rebuilding costs. The reader who thinks in systems will see the compounding mechanism.

stories.label: 'First contact' that may have led to complex life on Earth finally witnessed by scientists
stories.summary: Scientists in Australia's Shark Bay have for the first time witnessed the interaction between stromatolite microbes and more complex cellular organisms — the kind of 'first contact' thought to have triggered the evolution of complex life on Earth billions of years ago. The angle: this is a living window into one of the biggest transitions in evolutionary history, observed in real time in the same type of environment where it originally happened. Lead with the fact that this process was theorized but never seen — until now.

stories.label: 'It reads like a spy novel': $280 million theft from Drift involved North Korean fake companies, cutouts
stories.summary: North Korean operatives stole $280 million from crypto platform Drift using fake companies and cutouts — a six-month social engineering operation that started at a conference. The angle: this is how a sanctioned state funds itself. Lead with the tradecraft — fake quant-trading company, conference approach, six months of trust-building before the heist. The reader who builds software will recognize the social engineering pattern; the reader tracking North Korea will see the sanctions-evasion pipeline.

stories.label: France Launches Government Linux Desktop Plan as Windows Exit Begins
stories.summary: France has announced an official plan to migrate government desktops from Windows to Linux, framed as 'digital sovereignty' and reducing dependence on extra-European technology. The angle: this is the first major Western government to commit to a full Windows exit at the desktop level. Lead with the sovereignty framing — this isn't about cost savings, it's about a NATO ally deciding it can't depend on American software for government operations. The HN reader will debate feasibility; the geopolitics reader will see the pattern of decoupling.

stories.label: Israel bars Spain from US-led Gaza ceasefire monitoring centre
stories.summary: Netanyahu expelled Spain from the Gaza ceasefire monitoring centre hours after Madrid recognised Palestine and called for ICJ enforcement. The angle: Israel is systematically punishing states that use international law mechanisms — Spain, South Africa, Ireland, Colombia. Lead with the mechanism: this isn't a bilateral spat, it's a campaign to make the cost of recognising Palestinian rights higher than the cost of silence. The reader tracking accountability will see the pattern.

stories.label: European Airports Warn of Fuel Shortages if Gulf Supplies Remain Shut
stories.summary: European airport associations told EU officials that jet fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz must restart within three weeks or Europe faces 'systemic' aviation fuel shortages. The angle: the Iran war's economic damage is now threatening to ground flights across Europe. Lead with the 3-week deadline — this is a concrete, ticking clock that makes the abstract Hormuz closure tangible. The reader who tracked the Singapore air-con story will see the cascade widening to Europe's transport infrastructure.

stories.label: Court extends Activist Ahmed Douma's remand detention
stories.summary: An Egyptian court extended detention of prominent activist and writer Ahmed Douma for 15 more days on charges of 'spreading false news' — despite Douma having been previously granted a pardon. The angle: Egypt's pardon system is a revolving door. The state pardons activists for international optics, then re-arrests them on new charges. Lead with the pardon-then-redetain pattern — it reveals the machinery of controlled dissent. Douma has been a symbol of the 2011 revolution's unfinished promise.

stories.label: Hong Kong Grants First Stablecoin Licenses to HSBC, Standard Chartered-Backed Venture
stories.summary: Hong Kong issued its first stablecoin licenses to HSBC and a Standard Chartered-backed joint venture, marking a major step in Asia's digital asset regulation. The angle: while the US dithers on crypto regulation, Hong Kong is building the institutional rails. Colonial-era banks HSBC and StanChart are now the licensed issuers of Hong Kong dollar stablecoins — the old financial order absorbing the new. Lead with the institutional weight: these aren't crypto startups, they're the banks that built Asia's trade finance.

stories.label: The secret project to settle controversial maths proof with a computer
stories.summary: Two secret projects — working independently for over two years — are using formal verification software to settle the ABC conjecture, one of the most bitterly contested proofs in modern mathematics. Shinichi Mochizuki claimed to prove it in 2012; most mathematicians remain unconvinced. The angle: humans couldn't agree on whether the proof is valid, so now machines will arbitrate. Lead with the secrecy and the stakes — this is mathematics as a contact sport, and the computer is the referee neither side asked for.

stories.label: What's in a name? Moderna's "vaccine" vs. "therapy" dilemma
stories.summary: Moderna's personalised mRNA cancer treatment sequences a patient's tumour, identifies unique surface molecules (neoantigens), and trains the immune system to kill cells displaying them. It works like a vaccine — but calling it one triggers anti-vax backlash and regulatory confusion. The angle: the word 'vaccine' has become so politically toxic that it may slow adoption of a breakthrough cancer therapy. Lead with the mechanism (it IS a vaccine, technically) and the naming dilemma — the reader in tech will see the parallels to how framing shapes adoption of any new technology.

stories.label: Florida investigates OpenAI for role ChatGPT may have played in deadly shooting
stories.summary: Florida opened a state investigation into OpenAI after a gunman allegedly communicated extensively with ChatGPT in the days before a deadly shooting. The victim's family is also suing. The angle: this is the first state-level criminal investigation into an AI company's potential role in a killing — a regulatory precedent. Lead with the investigation (not the lawsuit) because state enforcement powers go further than civil liability. The reader building AI products needs to understand: the liability frontier just moved.
